speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While this is necessary if Singapore is to stay relevant and thrive, it is important for us to not lose focus on our foundation − the social structure on which we are built on and the values that have shaped us as a people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even as we transform our economy and workforce, we need also to strengthen families, reinforce values, such as family support and self-reliance, as well as nurture empathy and compassion within our community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, we need to continue supporting families of low income or unstable income, including families with retrenched workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we work towards helping them attain income stability and financial security, we must be ready to assist struggling families in a timely manner, before the situation gets out of hand, when it would be even more challenging to resolve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, we need to continue our support to ensure all children of Singapore, regardless of their family circumstances, will enjoy equal opportunities and good access to resources critical to their development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In recent years, I have been heartened by the changes made to ensure that all child-specific benefits are given to all Singaporean children, including children of unwed parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is precious help for the latter group.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, children of complex families and single-parent families still risk falling behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Amongst other disadvantages, they may lack proper guidance, good role models and a conducive home environment that allows them to focus on positive development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They risk developing restrictive world views, a distorted sense of how things work and habits detrimental to their future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When we speak of a conducive environment for children of more vulnerable backgrounds, I cannot help but also think about children of unwed parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These children, typically, are raised by one parent, usually the mother, who is the sole caregiver and sole breadwinner, and can only rely on the resources of this single parent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The unwed parent may often suffer strained relationships with his or her immediate family members and may be pressured to move out with the child, feeling unwanted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Prolonged absence of the other parent, pressures and the stigma of a child born out of wedlock and the risk of not having a proper, safe home all have an adverse impact on the child's development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can we help to ensure that these children will not feel unwanted, but that they are just as precious as any Singaporean child?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, we need to reinforce the values that shape and bind us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Values, such as family support and self-reliance, complemented by traits, such empathy and compassion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Values cultivation begins from the day we are born.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Schools play an indispensable role of educating and moulding minds, but nothing can fully substitute the role of parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the course of my constituency work, I have come to know two families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Family A is structurally intact, with a father, mother, three sisters and two young granddaughters.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Father is reluctant to work, despite being physically fit, preferring to subsist on donations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mother cannot work because her third daughter and two granddaughters are young children who need her care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Elder sister did not complete her education, could not hold down a job but does try to pay the bills, whilst waiting for her husband, who is a serial offender, to be released from prison.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Younger sister refuses to complete her education despite offers of bursaries, as her career "aspiration" is to make a quick buck exploiting her youth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Family B, however, is an unwed mother with five children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She has had her fair share of challenges trying to raise her children and make ends meet, with some financial assistance from us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But despite the very trying circumstances, her daughter Atiqa, who is now in Primary 2, aced her examinations and topped her class.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have known this family for years and I have witnessed how the mother cared for her children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She is not well educated but she made sure she is a very responsible mother.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When I was told of Atiqa's achievements during the Edusave Merit Education Awards earlier this year, I was so, so, so proud of her!

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Not only did Atiqa do well academically, her siblings are doing well in school as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At that moment, it struck me that responsible and good parenting makes a difference, a big difference, in who the children become.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I must say that parents play a key role in the family but, ironically, I think we all agree that while parenting is a big role, nothing quite prepares you for parenthood.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: MSF has initiated many family policies and programmes aimed at creating a total social environment conducive to family formation and the strengthening of family ties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With smaller families, apart from the various initiatives to increase centre-based services for child and student care, what support and programmes are in place to support parents in providing platforms to build stronger relationships within the families, including the importance of the role of both father and mother, in the care and development of their children?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As our population is rapidly ageing, as we look at strengthening the family, we must also give attention to how we support families in helping the seniors in families age well, as well as help families prepare and cope with the challenges of ageing, such as mental and emotional wellness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our families and seniors are important anchors of our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Strong families are the building blocks for strong communities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was recognised by this House in the debate on the Motion on Shared Values in 1991.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The late Dr Ong Chit Chung, my predecessor and mentor, said as follows in Parliament 26 years ago, "You may characterise the family as the building block of society, but I would rather call it the pillar of society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the pillar is eroded or weakened, society will not stand".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The family is the first place where we learn how to care for one another, to compromise and to maintain loving and respectful channels of communication.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The values that we learn within a family unit later transcends into how we interact with each other within our communities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Strong communities, in turn, cultivate a sense of belonging and support the basic framework of our resilience, competitiveness and quality of life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a framework that ensures a strong, caring and prosperous nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There can be no higher accolade for the recipients coming from the symbol of our nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our communities can also use the opportunity to celebrate these significant milestones with the families concerned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This symbolic act would be a tangible acknowledgment and appreciation of the sacrifices and contributions of our seniors and married couples within our families and community and a collective celebration of their life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will motivate and encourage others in our communities to emulate them, leading to a stronger community and nation for all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is by no means a novel suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Heads of states in other countries, such as the UK and US are already doing this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, we can have a unique Singapore adaptation to getting our community involved in celebrating these milestones.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The recent tightening of the regulatory framework to raise quality is another good move.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What else can an individual or centre operators do to contribute to the need for more manpower?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The scope of work can focus on child-minding, routine care of children and helping with early detection of symptoms of infectious diseases, such as Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease, or to look out for signs when a child is feeling unwell.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can also help with child-minding work on Saturdays, while the teachers concentrate on curriculum planning or attend training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This allied role will open up new job opportunities for the elderly and stay-at-home moms who wish to take up this kind of job.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most would be a good natural fit for the job as they would have relevant experiences and skillsets caring for their children or grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This registry can serve as an alternative solution for parents who are unable to take leave or seek childcare support from family members to care for their children when the kids are unwell or come down with infectious diseases, such as Hand, Foot and Mouth.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can ECDA coordinate with Government agencies to operate schemes and grants to help preschools tap on or work with partner vendors to set up systems, whether in the design of their programme or setting up apps to tie up for this thing of a registry of allied care-takers so that parents can gain access to resources to help them in minding their children?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is just the latest expansion in funding for this sector that we have seen over the last few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Finance Minister mentioned in his Budget Statement, the current capacity is already enough to accommodate more than half of all children between 18 months and six years of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond increases in capacity, the Government has also been focused on quality of childcare provision and the training of manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Just last week, the House passed the Early Childhood Development Centres Bill which will impose additional requirements on all kindergartens and childcare centres, including a stricter licensing regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite these increases, the strong growth in demand is likely to continue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As average household sizes fall, as the number of households with both parents working rises, and as older persons extend their participation in the workforce, childcare needs will have to be increasingly taken up by service providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is clearly a happy situation from a demographic perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even though we are far from reversing low birth rates, this indicates that a combination of efforts is making inroads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, the day-to-day situation is much more complex and full of coordination challenges for both parents and childcare providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: On the one hand, we have heard, as well as seen, rapid increases in demand for childcare and preschool services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Colleagues in this House often remind us that they come across working couples with young children who depend heavily on childcare and preschool support and, are very sensitive to gaps in supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One common situation we have heard of often occurs in new housing developments, when there is a lag between new childcare centres that commence operations and when residents shift into a development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This continuing growth will lead to an increase in pressure on skilled manpower, in competition with other sectors that have growing manpower needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the improved regulatory regime will no doubt increase the requirements, including manpower training, for operators in this sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Only one question: despite the fact that the excess capacity is a sign of responsiveness by the Government, it comes at a cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How has the Ministry been managing this cost?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This will allow parents to have peace of mind that their children are in good care while they are at work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To meet the demand, there has been a rapid increase and expansion of infant and childcare centres in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While capacity is important, what are the measures that the Ministry is taking to ensure that the quality of care is able to keep pace?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There has been focus on professional and career development to ensure qualified professionals for the sector.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can the Minister share what the progress has been in attracting and building the required talent base of professionals for this sector?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of my residents in the new BTOs told me that though they have shifted in, their children are still at their old place.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is because the childcare centre in the estate is not ready.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, for those few months, they have to keep sending the child to the old childcare centre which could be in another part of Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry work with HDB to hand over the block with the childcare centre earlier, so that ECDA and the operator have time to set up the childcare centre?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even when the childcare centre is ready, these parents are not guaranteed a place.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, some parents are not able to enrol their children in the nearest centre.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For parents who do not drive, it is time-consuming to send their children to centres that are not near their homes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they have two or three children under different care arrangements in different locations, then the problem is even greater.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Ministry can work with HDB to review the provision of childcare spaces in new BTOs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from operators that the difficulty in expanding is the shortage of preschool teachers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Very often, they have the space but then they cannot take in so many students and this could be due to their salary being less than school teachers, even if both are graduates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is more, preschool teachers have to bathe and clean up after the children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is no wonder that many graduates and diploma holders do not want to become preschool teachers or quit shortly after joining.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Ministry can look into this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to ask the Minister whether there will be any more mega centres setting up in Nee Soon because I have a lot of residents telling me that they have difficulty in getting a childcare centre?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more women and grandparents enter or remain in the workforce, the demand for infant care and childcare increases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to build a strong system of caregiving support to help young married couples in their parenthood journey.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, parents with children in childcare and infant care centres benefit from a basic subsidy and an additional subsidy which help offset the centres' fees.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help these families cope with the higher expenses incurred in looking after more children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to appeal for an increase in the provision of childcare and infant care facilities in Sengkang South.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the face of the uncertain future economy and global competition, it is likely that lower income families will be affected more.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Parents from low-income families may be struggling with day-to-day expenses and may have very little time, money or energy left to focus on things like enrichment or additional classes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These enrichment classes I am referring to are not only those for the children, but for the parents, too, like parenting skills or courses that will help them develop their children's potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they are not able to invest in these classes, their children may, in the long run, lose out because of the stiff competition in the world today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should ensure that these families have access to as many programmes without having to worry about the cost so that their children can be as equipped as the children from a better-off family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This was a pilot programme introduced last year to provide upstream support to low-income and vulnerable children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may still be too early to assess the effectiveness of the programme but I believe that any effort to help strengthen the capabilities of low-income families and help their children move up the social ladder is a good effort.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are there plans to enhance the programme in the future and reach out to a bigger group?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think it is useful to consider replicating these efforts beyond the pilot programme so that we could also collectively learn from experiences with different groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would also ask that the Ministry consider developing a template possibly that could be rolled out to various constituencies so that more families can benefit from such programmes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some children are being looked after by their extended families when their parent or parents are in prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These children are often neglected and have poor school attendance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Kindergarten Fee Assistance Scheme (KiFAS), which provides assistance to some of these families, currently requires, a minimum school attendance of one day a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What other measures are being taken to ensure that these children receive adequate schooling?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our current policy appears to penalise stay-at-home mothers since they receive less subsidies for infant care and childcare as compared to working mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does seem odd to provide more financial subsidies for working mothers who have an income and provide less financial subsidies for stay-at-home mothers who do not have an income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we level the playing field and not penalise parents who choose to spend more time with their children and sacrifice their careers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: These are parents who have family members or caregivers from their neighbourhoods who can help to look after their babies and children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: To ensure that these caregivers meet standards in caring for young ones, the Ministry can organise a training and certification process for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Those who pass the training will then be entitled to the grants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: People who provide such freelance care-giving services for children should be supported as professionals, too.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is also limited by how much more we can build.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While it is essential to continue investing in these areas to enhance our social safety net, we need to balance this by enabling our elderly to age successfully at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I know this is for those with disabilities, but the learnings can be equally relevant for the caring of our elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With a smaller family unit, the responsibility of caring for our elderly will fall on the shoulders of a smaller pool of individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can we encourage a shared caregiving model within our communities?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that caregivers should be given courses on how and what it takes to care for the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The caregivers who have to work should be further aided with digital apps.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The apps are to be linked to intelligent sensors and gadgets that are installed at home or worn on the elderly to indicate their conditions, for example, in cases of falls, or for them to provide reminders for medication.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These notifications can be sent to the caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The community can also play a part and serve as connectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But who are the connectors and how can they contribute?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Connectors are the family members, students, community groups and healthcare partners.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We can begin with training the healthy and socially-active seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They can contribute significantly when we help to connect them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, they have the Community Engagement Programme (CEP), but I feel that the focus is diluted and the purpose of doing it is not well communicated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I suggest to refocus and begin with the Secondary and tertiary students.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Allow them to focus their engagement in different neighbourhoods with elderly-related topics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will help build stronger bonds within the communities and encourage our young to participate in active volunteerism.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I state my interest as a director in a social business involved in youth training and development.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I read reports last year that the number of drug abusers under 30 years old is growing in Singapore and that the young drug abuser profile is also evolving and more of them are actually academically successful students from middle to high income households.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, anecdotally, other forms of risky behaviours, like self-mutilation, anorexia and online gambling, have also been gaining traction among young people for some years.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our current solutions feature public educational talks and materials, but many young people can share with you that just telling them not to do something and telling them why it is bad for them does not work and does not get to the root of their problems.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: From my training experience, I can confirm this: nobody changes just by being told a solution at the intellectual level of the head.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: People change fundamentally only when they experience the solution as an emotional connection in the heart and a physical connection in their body.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is as true for the young students as much as for the adult professionals that we train.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I propose that we explore an alternative approach to solving the risky behavioural problems of our youths by following what Iceland has already done to tremendous success.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are a small country, just like us, and I believe we can see similar success as them if we give their model a shot.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Twenty years ago, Iceland faced a severe troubled teen crisis.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their youths were among the heaviest-drinking youths in Europe.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Smoking, drug abuse and other forms of risky behaviour were actually quite prevalent.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But, today, Iceland boasts some of Europe's cleanest-living teens.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Icelandic model is based on the research of American psychologist Harvey Milkman.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: His theory was that it was not the different versions of self-harm themselves that people were getting addicted to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: He discovered that what people were addicted to were the specific changes in brain chemistry that were induced by these actions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And their harmful behaviours of choice were linked to their preferred coping mechanisms of dealing with stress.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those who preferred to numb their stress away would choose solutions like heroin, sedatives or alcohol.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And those who preferred to actively confront their stress would use solutions like stimulant drugs or online gambling.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The programme did not tell the teenagers, "You're going to come in for treatment." It simply told them, "We are here to teach you anything you want to learn − music, art, dance, martial arts, hip-hop." And these classes were deliberately curated to provide youths a wide variety of alterations in brain chemistry and give them alternative solutions to cope better with life's stresses.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those who liked to numb their stress could go for experiences that reduced anxiety, like painting or yoga, and those who liked to confront their stress could go for experiences that provided a sudden rush, like karate or hip hop.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In 1991, Harvey Milkman started going to Iceland regularly to share about his findings and Iceland was so taken by his research that they started to run it on a national level.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The first thing that they did was gather fresh and specific data.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, in 1992, every school in Iceland got their 14 to16-year-olds to fill in a questionnaire with questions like, "Have you tried alcohol?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If so, when did you last have your drink?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Do you have a close relationship with your parents?" This questionnaire was repeated in 1995 and 1997.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Then, they drilled into the data to identify precisely which schools had the worst problems and which had the least.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their analysis revealed clear differences between the lives of kids who self-harmed and those who did not.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Kids who stayed away from risky behaviours were those who participated in organised activities, especially sports, three or four times a week.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They were also the ones who felt cared for at school, spent more time with parents during the week and were home during the late evenings.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the survey data, a new national plan was gradually introduced.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Laws were changed to make purchase of alcohol and drugs more difficult.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Parental organisations were to be established in every school.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: State funding was increased for organised sports and arts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Most crucially, the surveys were continued and updated.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Each year, almost every child in Iceland completes one.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, in Iceland, up-to-date, reliable data on where youths are currently, is always available.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Icelandic researchers have a saying "Like vegetables, information has to be fresh." As well as fresh, information has to be local, so that schools, parents and officials can see exactly where the problems exist in which areas.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Iceland's turnaround is innovative, evidence-based and remarkably common-sensical.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope very much to see a national level "Youth in Singapore" questionnaire done sometime soon.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because I think it will give us fresh year-on-year data to create an always relevant and powerful programme of alternative stress-relievers for all our kids to experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For families whose relationships have weakened due to various circumstances, parents may face challenges in providing the appropriate care and environment for their children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is the programme supporting vulnerable families stay together?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What services have been established to provide support to vulnerable children to allow them to stay in safe family environments?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Our demographics, in terms of families, are changing and our economy is changing as well.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: This confluence places great stress and pressure on families and this may strain relationships.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: It is important that we keep our family ties strong.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What are MSF's plans to identify vulnerable families and intervene to strengthen the relationship and prevent escalation to family violence?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What programmes are there to guide, counsel and support family members?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am concerned about the families I met who are unable to get out of debt, sometimes even after receiving Government help.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, I am not speaking about families who owe money, that run into hefty amounts due to business failure or gambling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am referring to families who are often in arrears for phone, utilities, rental, mortgage payments and simply cannot make ends meet because of their low income, or debt burdens left by spouses, or debts accumulated due to inaction.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The current financial help that MSF's Social Service Office (SSO) offers may not solve this debt spiral.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the possible reasons is that the formula that is used usually does not factor in a needy beneficiary's financial liability status when computing the help quantum.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I can understand why the state would not want to use taxpayers' money to solve financial mismanagement issues of other citizens.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SSO officers themselves may also not be trained in financial counselling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the effect of ignoring this is that the family continues to be in a state of poverty, impairing their ability to get out of the spiral.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When they cannot clear their debts, they simply borrow more to make ends meet, getting deeper into debt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But in the absence of bonuses like this, I would like to make two suggestions to the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, develop a "Turn-key Solution" for families of this profile.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many times, the persons in debt have to work this out themselves and they often give up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Do not pack them off to general money management courses or send them to an external Financial Counsellor.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Help them work out a financial debt redemption plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At times, it may mean being more generous also, in the financial help given directly to assist dependants, such as their children and their elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, work with partners and develop creative "Get-out-of-Debt" Schemes that will incentivise affected families to clear their debts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another could be creating flexible job opportunities to allow them to work part-time to earn some extra cash.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Regarding Temporary Assistance, I would like to clarify how the Government tracks its success.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it simply based on the number of persons helped, or is there tracking as to how many persons managed to attain self-sufficiency to no longer need the scheme?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Based on the cases I have encountered, there seems to be a rule or guideline that, after a number of months, the quantum of help is reduced and then help is refused altogether.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I support the rationale of incentivising persons to be self-sufficient, we sometimes see families stricken with illness and mental problems who have limited means of helping themselves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the Public Assistance allowance of $500 for a single person is meant for the person to defray his living expenses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PA allowance is usually given in a cash lump sum, from which the recipient is expected to pay his bills, such as rent, utilities and Town Council S&CC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is different from those on Temporary Assistance, where the Government commonly makes direct payment of utilities and S&CC bills to agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many on Public Assistance are elderly and/or permanently unable to work, are usually not in robust health and have no relatives to help them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be more efficient for the Long-Term Assistance scheme to make direct payment to the relevant agencies?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, there are SMTA recipients who still struggle with additional expenses and who have few alternatives to turn to.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Although SMTA is able to cover basic daily expenses, it is still lacking in terms of ad hoc big-ticket expenses, for example, repairing of damaged household appliances or items and repairing damaged spectacles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: These are expenses that do not occur daily but can rack up substantial costs when they do.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This can be modelled on the discretionary assistance under Public Assistance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am putting up two recommendations for consideration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: By allowing only up to 70% claim for annual repairs allowance, recipients still have to take responsibility for 30% of the expenses and the annual cap prevents excessive spending and abuse of the system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, a more in-depth review should also be done to understand the amounts that these groups have to fork out for such expenses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This can have a maximum lifetime cap of up to $300 per recipient.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: For one-off claims, it will be administratively more efficient to allow a 100% claim, since it is only a one-time funding and cannot be reclaimed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This is to emulate part of discretionary assistance under PA to extend additional coverage support for SMTA recipients who are unable to qualify for additional welfare programmes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I would appreciate if the Minister can provide updates on the SSO meeting its objectives, in particular, its role in integrating social service delivery.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In addition, I have two questions and one suggestion to make.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: First, in reply to my 2013 Parliamentary Question (PQ) on whether SSO will be staffed by social work-trained officers and what is the proposed number, the Ministry mentioned that some of the staff may have social work training.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It was further mentioned that the Ministry will provide the requisite training to enable all staff to perform their roles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am asking this because I have come across many such cases where these young parents are receiving financial assistance from SSO but came to me to seek help with childcare placement.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As for my suggestion, can each SSO produce a mini directory with a map on all the social and community services available within its boundary so as to better assist residents, especially elderly residents	to locate the services?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, last year, my colleague, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested establishing a Commissioner for the maintenance of families, empowered to recover maintenance on behalf of families and provide means-tested support where needed during the process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Department of Human Services Child Support in Australia can collect child support payments on behalf of the parent, investigate cases of non-payment and issue overseas travel bans, amongst other actions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UK, too, has a child maintenance service that is empowered to take action against the defaulting party if maintenance is not paid.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our system, the onus still lies mainly on the claimant to make trips to Court to enforce the maintenance order.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can take a toll on the emotional well-being of spouses who are affected and may even affect their earning power if they have to repeatedly take leave from work to make visits to the Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current enforcement process is one that punishes claimants with unrepentant or spiteful ex-spouses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A central agency would help relieve this unjust burden.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister share more details on this office, including the staff and number of investigations that have commenced and concluded, as well as an assessment of the initial impact?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, the Government has enabled unwed mothers to be given the same 16-week maternity leave that all mothers get in Singapore as well as a Child Development Account.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should, however, still seek to provide a complete ecosystem of support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are also not able to buy an HDB flat as they are deemed to not have a family nucleus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, they can only buy a flat under the Singles Scheme or from the resale market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, under the Singles Scheme, they get smaller grants, compared to first-time married couples.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unwed mothers who need a home to bring up a child will find it challenging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could we re-look at the definition of a family nucleus so that unwed mothers can be granted with full housing grant and truly make it "Happy Women's Day".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We often say that the family is the "bedrock of society".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In our ideal conception, family is where people are cared and provided for, protected and loved.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are many people who do these things every day − for their spouse, their partner, their children, their parents.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in the eyes of our laws and Government policies, they do not fit into the conventional and official definition of family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These are single parents, unwed mothers, foreign wives, cohabiting same-sex couples, and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because they do not qualify as family, access to basic necessities, like housing, is a real problem.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Single parents and children shuttle from one temporary home to another, live in overcrowded units and not having personal space to study and play are undesirable to a child's development.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Not belonging to a heterosexual, nuclear family is not a personal failing − relationships fail, partners die, some are just not that into the opposite gender.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to make inclusive policies for family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These children will not inherit from their father's estate if the father dies without a will.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They can inherit from their mother only if she has no other children from within a marriage.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are also tax reliefs that are available only to married mothers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has said that the distinctions are there to promote "strong marriages" and the norms of family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But is it really true that people will cultivate aspirations and norms based on these challenging technicalities?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The only real effect these policies have is to disadvantage some families by making their affairs more burdensome to manage and also stigmatise the children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Ground experiences from VWOs working with single parents show that housing policies are hard to understand and that there is a lack of coordination between Ministries and Departments to provide support for families in transition who are usually in a stressful situation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Dealing with complicated policies or having to navigate the system adds to the stress.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It could function as a one-stop shop where, for example, divorced parents can go to for assistance on legal matters, advice on housing options, post-divorce and child welfare-related services.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a classroom, the students were once asked to make images of an ideal family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A group of male students formed this image: two guys sitting in front; two guys standing behind.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, the classmates asked, "Who played the mother?" Refusing to be seen as playing a female character, the male student said, "We are all males!" Some asked, "How come ideal family got no mother?" Then a student spoke up, "Why can this not be an ideal family?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Father, uncle, two brothers." It was a very strong plea by this student, for whatever reason, this image meant a lot to her.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And, so, I urge our policies not to bring further harm and hurt to these families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is possibly because of the talks conducted at the grassroots level on these matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have met some elderly residents who do not have children or family members whom they can depend on when they are no longer healthy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Naturally, some would have concerns about their options and what they can do to make the necessary preparation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Mental Capacity Act was amended last year to introduce the broad framework on professional donees and professional deputies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This was a very important move, in light of difficulties faced by the elderly who may not have any family members or close friends to rely on to make arrangements when he or she loses mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: During the debates on the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Bill, the Minister acknowledged the need for robust registration criteria and regulation of professional deputies and donees.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There were also concerns raised about the costs that may be charged by these professionals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In addition, could more be done to ensure access to services to the elderly, especially those without next-of-kin, to help them prepare and plan for the situation when they lose capacity and are not able to care for themselves?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Lily Neo, you can take both your cuts together.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The social problem of "abuse of vulnerable adults" is unacceptable in any society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have spoken in Parliament on this topic many a time since 1999.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The earlier we can have the Vulnerable Adults Act, the better.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In many cases of abuse, the best way to end their plight is to remove the vulnerable seniors from their homes and place them at designated facilities that can provide better support and care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is for fear of losing whatever little care and support they are getting that many vulnerable adults rather suffer in silence and not report their predicament.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, whilst we intend to have the Vulnerable Adults Act in place, we need to ensure that alternative assistance is also readily available to them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a pity that very few people will come forward to report cases of abuse.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This may be due to lack of awareness, fear of being worse off without their own families or being afraid of their liabilities, especially with Court proceedings.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the Vulnerable Adults Act will change this.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF start raising awareness of elderly abuse?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Has there been a study on the prevalence of elderly abuse?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF publish the prevalence of elderly abuse cases in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Knowledge about cases of abuse is often limited to some family members, neighbours and friends.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We can help more of these abuse cases only when more people are made aware of elderly abuse, its prevalence and what help is available.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: And for a start, we need a facility for easy one-stop reporting and good follow-up by MSF.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Social workers are seeing more seniors being cheated or financially abused by their children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF start equipping seniors on abuses, especially financial abuse, as a first step to assist seniors to safeguard their money?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What kind of assistance can MSF provide to such cases who seek help?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MSF consider setting up a bureau to investigate, mediate and counsel the parties involved following complaints of abuse?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MSF enable the bureau, if all else fails, to prosecute the offenders for abuse of the elderly?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially so for seniors living alone in HDB rental flats.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They usually do not have family members to depend on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Has there been any "needs analysis study" done to ascertain the vulnerable seniors requiring assistance for various reasons, such as financial need, daily living difficulty, loneliness and depression?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Would MSF extend comprehensive social assistance to the vulnerable seniors, especially those with mobility disability, to enable them to age gracefully in their own homes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Although the causes of suicides are often multi-factorial and they include physical and mental illness and social isolation, the latter, leading to loneliness and depression in seniors, is one of the more important contributing factors for the seniors here to take their own lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Long-term social isolation may also result in deterioration of physical well-being and health.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors, especially the frail ones, usually prefer not to go out of their own homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, having volunteers and befrienders visiting them will be helpful.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF implement measures to combat loneliness amongst the seniors as part of comprehensive assistance to vulnerable seniors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The challenge is how to ensure a steady stream of volunteers, especially those who are willing to commit long-term and build lasting relationships with seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Having befrienders who stay for a long time makes for greater continuity.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is this kind of relationship that the seniors value.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Funds are needed for the running and training costs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: More mature jobseekers and able-bodied seniors, especially those who are interested to contribute back to society, can be recruited as permanent befrienders.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MSF can encourage this group of befrienders by providing a reasonable amount of allowance for them to befriend seniors closer to their homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Volunteers can go through training sessions to understand basic know-how at identifying any potential psychological issues, such as suicidal thoughts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Volunteers can also be taught how to refer the seniors they visit for social needs like food delivery, financial assistance, home help or medical escorts and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MSF can collaborate with other Ministries, such as MOH, VWOs and companies for better coordination of services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Young families who wish to inculcate good values, such as filial piety, in their children might consider visiting the seniors on a regular basis as a befriender family.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF facilitate "adopt a grandparent" scheme by families?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: On the group of persons with disability, will MSF enlighten this House on the Enabling Masterplan 3?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Government plan to build an ecosystem of support for persons with disabilities?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I want to thank the Minister, the Ministry, the Steering Committee chaired by Ms Anita Fam, and my fellow Steering Committee members and all who made this possible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The Masterplan is an important milestone for our nation-building because Singapore is neither just an economy nor a corporation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If Singapore is to be a home worth defending, then every citizen born to it is worth valuing, regardless of race, religion or abilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The EM3 was intentionally broad in its directions and recommendations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There is more to be uncovered, more to be added, especially in the light of a need for a 21st century social services sector in an age of digitalisation, disruption and sea changes in demographics.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: To me, leaving the EM3 plan to be interpreted and rolled out solely by the Government, seeking inputs and reporting only when it wishes, is not a wise and progressive strategy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This self-check and self-reporting mode will reduce the transparency and trust that the Ministry has diligently built up in the last decade.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Of course, who would want to install a body to check on itself, but this is a Government Ministry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This Committee should comprise key members of the EM3 Steering Committee representing the key disability groups and representatives from other EM3-Implementing Ministries and agencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Just as there is a strong need for self-driven and innovative enterprises and learners in the economy of the future, so should the social service of the future start to transform itself.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There will never be sufficient public resources to meet the needs of all the disability groups, in the face of so many competing demands of the displaced, the rapidly ageing and other disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We need to enable, recognise and nurture self-driven and innovative disability groups.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The Ministry should encourage the key disability groups to start developing their own Enabling Plans so that their highest priority needs can be identified, implemented with support from parties which do not only include the Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: These mini plans are not mere inputs of the randomly assembled focus groups; their content will provide good inputs for the accurate and impactful roll-out of the Enabling Masterplan in the next five years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Suggestion three − develop a more comprehensive profiling of caregivers and needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Caregiver needs differ, depending on the age of child, age of parents, education level, interest, disability and age of the charges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The history of caregiver support in the disability sector has been dotted with centralisation and decentralisation, with the DIRC, Centre for Enabled Living, SG Enable and also the whole Caregiver Support Centre networks in, for example, Asian Women's Welfare Association (AWWA) and Rainbow Centre.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I feel strongly the need for caregiver needs to be more carefully analysed and segmented according to demographic and disability profiles.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We should not spend resources setting up yet another Caregiver Centre or Village.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Existing hubs, such as SG Enable, can coordinate and equip current centres and increase more accessible touch-points at the hospitals, schools, VWOs and even SSOs and community centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Suggestion four − develop a more systematic and structured way to rope in community helpers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There ought to be a more structured and effective way to organise a stronger and more consistent community volunteer and help network, involving neighbouring schools, corporations, grassroots and residents in the precinct.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: To me, a vast resource to tap on.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I suggest that the school-to-work scheme be independently reviewed to determine its strengths and areas of weaknesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I understand that the scheme has strong merit because it is well resourced and has the ability to tap on a network of corporate partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, I hear it needs to be improved because of less than structured support and follow-up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There is room for MOE, MSF and SG Enable to tap on the current job assessment and placement centres with MINDS, Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and Autism Resource Centre (ARC) so that there can be more structure, streamlining and continuity after the students graduate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For the more severe trainees, there is also strong merit for the Ministry and its agents to bring back a more updated version of sheltered enterprises that could create piece-meal paid work so that those with moderate to severe needs need not adopt the more costly options of staying at home or using a day care service.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I have personally witnessed programmes like these which are very successful and I am sure we can scale some of these models for this target group.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Suggestion six − take a deep-dive review of the real needs of adults with moderate to severe needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Conclusion − finally, Sir, the clarion call in the digital economy of the future is just as loud for special needs, for the social service sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Nonetheless, I am very grateful that Singapore has our own Masterplan and that I am able to share my proposals for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Chairman, while we restructure the economy to be vibrant, let us also continue to help our disabled jobseekers and their needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: SG Enable's open-door programme has helped many Singaporeans with training and jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry also update on the latest progress?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Are there enough positions to meet the demand?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Which sector has been the most progressive in hiring Singaporeans with special needs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Acceptance and opening our office doors to Singaporeans with disabilities require a shared appreciation of each other's capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This must be ingrained from the very start.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I encourage creating funding and platforms for our schools and youths to start joint projects where the disabled and able-bodied youths will get the opportunity to work together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Through these activities and interactions, mutual respect and understanding can germinate early, reaping returns of greater inclusivity at the workplace at the later stages.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Somebody who is diagnosed with special needs or has a disability from a young age will use up the grant much faster than a person who is diagnosed later in life, as will a person whose disability may require more expensive assistive devices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The purpose of the fund will be better served if it can be made more flexible to take into consideration the lifetime needs of individuals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It is also stated that after the approval of an application to use the fund, touchpoints such as hospitals and VWOs, will assist individuals to purchase the devices and reimbursement will either be made to the touchpoint or to the vendor.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are shocked and saddened when a person ends his or her life.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But it is even sadder when it is a parent who ends his or her life, as well as the life of a disabled child.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But for every life ended, hundreds and thousands of people, caregivers and parents plough on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Pressure builds until it becomes unbearable and then enough is enough.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And, so, before it is too late, caregivers must be cared for.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They live difficult lives, painful lives, for love.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And while I think that support groups are important, I doubt that caregivers will want to spend their free time revolving around support groups.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that caregivers would want to spend "me" time and have the confidence that, as they spend "me" time, the disabled child, sibling or parent will be well looked after − to have "me" time without the guilt, without the worry; to plan their time off, without guilt, without worry.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to hearing from the Minister on my question as filed.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Disability Caregiver Support Centre playing a differentiated role from what it is already offered by VWOs − a role that is insightful, impactful and empathetic in strengthening and powering caregivers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Desmond Choo, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Having a pipeline of quality manpower in this sector is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry look at shortening the training period for prospective entrants without compromising the necessary depth of training?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: (In Mandarin):   A career in childcare or social services is very meaningful.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Yet, many workers have told me that the remuneration and opportunities for career development lag behind other professions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This may become a barrier, as many new entrants decide to switch jobs so that they can establish a good economic foundation for themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Hence, I would like to suggest that we actively promote a shared-services business model which can do away with unnecessary expenses, and benefits can be shared with the workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This will not only strengthen organisational capabilities, but also help better childcare and social service centres expand quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The Government can work with social enterprises under the union movement to promote this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Helping those with special needs speaks of the conscience and grace of our nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Both corporations and the larger community have important roles in weaving our tapestry of social hope and support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The SHARE as One programme is a meaningful platform for Singaporeans to give towards charities through their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It also helps companies to build CSR programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Government provide an update on the scheme?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Are there plans to further enhance the scheme?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: A growing group that requires support are parents of autistic children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Anecdotally, children might wait for a year or more to get into a special education or SPED school or centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: As these families have to cope with the high cost of raising the child, could subsidies or greater tax considerations be given to them?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The community which embraces special needs persons is critical to making Singapore inclusive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry also share on other public education and outreach programmes they have, to educate the public about autism and the challenges in raising an autistic child?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Would the Ministry also consider the further implementation of the very popular and successful inclusive playgrounds in the heartlands?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this number is still far from what Singapore needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Social workers play an integral role in alleviating the problems faced by vulnerable members of our society and they deserve remuneration that reflects the job complexity and high amounts of stress they face in their line of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though the Government has pledged to review and provide salary guidelines "based on market data and benchmarks", it is not clear exactly how the benchmarking is conducted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Back when the Government was looking to make teaching an attractive profession, it raised the salaries of teachers and increased the quality of their training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I ask that the Government do the same for social workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to appeal to the Government for transparency in the salary benchmarking process and to set a timeline for regular wage reviews for social workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, many sceptics doubt these measures are sufficient to moderate the cost of living and believe that consumers will take the brunt of the price increase.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is fear that cost increases can potentially spiral and this should be addressed in two prongs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First, to ensure that sellers are not exploiting and profiteering from the situation; and, second, to educate the people to be prudent in all aspects of their daily consumption.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The sandwiched class is usually the most affected but given the least support.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These are the mid-level professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) − the new vulnerable group of people, both in terms of securing employment and managing the family's cost of living.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Government can provide more short-term support for this group, especially when the economic prospect looks bleak with lower employment rate.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I am glad that the Ministry will be doing more to help caregivers and assisting people with disabilities find work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The third Enabling Masterplan aims to better integrate people with disabilities into the workforce by giving more support to caregivers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is the joint effort and initiative by the committee comprising both private and public sector representatives.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Disability Caregiver Support Centre is one promising initiative.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I do hope that more can be done in assisting people with disabilities gain employment so that they can earn a dignified living.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For this, we will need corporate organisations to support the employment of people with not just mild disability but also moderate disabilities.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: My personal experience working with people with disabilities has been a promising one.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They are consistent, reliable and diligent; performing well in their given job scope.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: SG Enable has instituted programmes to create awareness among companies and conduct training for potential corporate organisations which show a keen interest in hiring people with disabilities.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We must applaud such organisations for their willingness and pursuit to do good in Corporate Social Responsibility.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In an effort to attract and retain talents, will the funding for VWOs-Charities Capability Fund be used to provide staff with training and better remuneration, especially for VWOs-Charities that provide some form of healthcare services?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we can enhance the attractiveness of the sector, strengthen ability and build up the Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was stated that NCSS intends to help these VWOs strengthen their organisations and develop alternative resources to support their functions.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Hougang has been blessed with the presence of these small charities.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure these outfits are doing good work in other parts of Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These smaller VWOs are able to complement and contribute to the collective effort of big charities and the Ministry to help needy Singaporeans in filling the gaps and providing very targeted assistance at times.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They are able to reach out to the needy at a personal level and with great speed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thus, I wish to seek an update from the Ministry on the reported effort to help these smaller charities serve the community.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What are the possible alternative ways to help them raise the much-needed funds effectively?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was reported that grassroots organisations raised about $7 million from community trade fairs in the last financial year.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The GROs were also given $206 million to spend the same year.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would the Ministry consider allowing smaller VWOs to raise funds through trade fairs instead, as these charities do not have many opportunities to raise meaningful donations effectively?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Giving the trade fair quotas to these VWOs will also help bring awareness to their presence in the community and the good work they have done to serve the needy residents there.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: However, given the limited resources and the limited expertise of VWOs in applying for grants and engaging competent service providers.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Providing a helping hand should not just be the job of social workers or VWOs.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I believe all of us can be our brothers or sisters' keepers.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As we continue to professionalise the social service sector, what are the plans to tap on the wider community of volunteers?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Volunteers can supplement the tight manpower in the social service sector.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I hope we can empower and encourage more Singaporeans to play a part, no matter how small, to reach out to Singaporeans in need of assistance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Likewise, a community plays an important role in caring for the vulnerable and in engendering social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But it is increasingly important for practical reasons, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Even with new workforce entrants, there will always be stiff competition for manpower.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But with calls for more and higher quality programmes to address unfulfilled needs, the need for people will only increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The community has so far demonstrated how we can organise ourselves and achieve many things.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We have corporates and residents who have diverse skillsets and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: They may also have the capacity outside of work and family time to help.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to thank Members of the House for the suggestions on making Singapore a more caring society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: My Ministry is on a constant lookout for new ways to make our social support system more responsive to the changing needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The global economy is slowing and we expect greater uncertainties in the labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Naturally, some of us may be concerned about the challenges in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In the coming years, my Ministry's efforts will remain focused on these three areas.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: First, we will stay committed towards building an inclusive society in Singapore where no one will be left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Second, we will also work on strengthening families so that families can continue to serve as a pillar of support for individuals and the basic building block of society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Third, we will continue to enhance the capabilities of the people sector, so that they can continue to do good work for our community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We believe that for those who can work, apart from tiding them over difficult times in the short term, the best support we can provide for them is to enable them to find and sustain work.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Only then can they be empowered to improve the situation of their families and themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will try to do this through our Social Service Offices (SSOs).

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The majority of our SSOs now are standalone SSOs that are not co-located with WSG and e2i.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: At these SSOs, appointments are made for clients requiring employment assistance to see WSG or e2i officers who come down to the SSOs once a week.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: At some SSOs, the wait time can be two to three weeks or more.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
